title: Everyday Computers and Smartphones
summary: By the end, learners can name everyday digital devices, use basic on-screen actions, find files in folders, connect to Wi-Fi with more care, and describe simple habits that help keep a computer or phone safer.

lessons.title: Meet your everyday devices
lessons.html:
A digital device is a tool that stores and shares information. Canada’s Skills for Success program calls digital skill the ability to use digital technology and tools to find, manage, apply, create, and share information and content. That includes computers, tablets, smartphones, and other handheld devices.

Common devices:

  • A desktop computer usually stays on a desk and uses a separate screen, keyboard, and mouse.
  • A laptop is a portable computer with a built-in screen and keyboard.
  • A tablet is a flat screen you control mostly by touch.
  • A smartphone is a phone that also works like a small computer. Get Cyber Safe notes that people use phones as cameras, maps, and more — not only to make calls.

You do not need to own every device. Many libraries and adult learning centres have computers you can practise on.

Shared ideas on most devices:

  • A screen shows what is happening.
  • You give commands by tapping, clicking, or typing.
  • Settings (sometimes a gear icon) let you change things such as volume, brightness, or Wi-Fi.
  • Apps or programs are tools you open to do a job, such as mail, maps, or a web browser.

Skills for Success also asks learners to know basic words that most devices share, and to use basic functions that are common to most of them. If a word is new, write it down and ask a tutor. Learning the names helps you follow instructions later.

This course will not repair a broken device. If something will not turn on, check the power or charger first, then ask for help.

lessons.title: Turn on, look around, and lock the screen
lessons.html:
Before you learn programs, get comfortable with the device in front of you.

Start up. Press the power button until the screen lights up. Wait. The first screen may ask you to swipe, tap, or type a password, PIN, or use a fingerprint. Get Cyber Safe says to give a computer a strong log-in password and to lock it when you are not around. On a phone or tablet, use a lock-screen password and turn on extra lock options, such as a fingerprint, if they are available. Also turn on auto-lock so the device locks after a short time.

Look around.

  • On a computer, the mouse or trackpad moves a pointer. A single click usually selects something. A double-click often opens it.
  • On a phone or tablet, a light tap often opens an item. Swipe to move around the screen.
  • The keyboard (physical or on-screen) is for typing.

If you open the wrong thing, look for a Back arrow, an X to close a window, or the Home button or gesture on a phone. Skills for Success includes knowing when to use Back and Next, and how to scroll.

Lock when you step away. Even at home, locking the screen helps keep photos, messages, and files private. Do not write a password on a sticky note beside the device. Get Cyber Safe says never to write a password down and then store it near the computer, and never to share your password with anyone.

Practise turning the device on, unlocking it with help from a tutor if needed, opening one app, closing it, and locking the screen again.

lessons.title: Files, folders, and finding your work
lessons.html:
A file is one piece of saved work, such as a letter, a photo, or a spreadsheet. A folder is a container that holds files (and sometimes other folders). Skills for Success includes storing and organizing digital information in a logical way using files, folders, and labels — for example, downloading a file into a folder on your computer.

On a Windows computer, File Explorer helps you find, open, organize, and manage files and folders. Microsoft’s help says you can open File Explorer from the taskbar or the Start menu, or by pressing the Windows logo key and the letter E.

Common folders you may see include Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Music, and Videos. Many apps save everyday files into one of these folders, which makes them easier to find later.

Habits that help:

  1. Give a file a clear name you will remember, such as rent-receipt-november rather than document1.
  2. Save related files in the same folder.
  3. Use the search box in File Explorer if you forget where a file went. Microsoft says you can search from File Explorer Home, or search inside a folder such as Downloads.
  4. To move a file, Microsoft’s File Explorer help says to select it, choose Cut, go to the new place, then choose Paste.

On a phone, files may sit in Photos, Files, Downloads, or inside an app. The idea is the same: know where you saved something.

Ask a tutor before you permanently delete a file you might still need.

lessons.title: Connect to the internet with care
lessons.html:
The internet lets your device visit websites, send messages, and use many apps. A common way to connect is Wi-Fi.

On Windows 11, Microsoft’s steps are: select the Network, Sound, or Battery icons on the taskbar to open quick settings; on the Wi-Fi setting, choose Manage Wi-Fi connections; pick the network you want; select Connect; then type the network password and select Next. On Windows 10, select the Network icon on the taskbar, choose the network, select Connect, and type the password.

Use a network you trust, such as your home Wi-Fi or a network a staff person names at the learning centre. Get Cyber Safe warns that public Wi-Fi is convenient but less safe. Anyone can join, including people who should not see your information. Criminals sometimes set up fake hotspots with a name that looks almost real. When you can, ask someone at the place hosting the Wi-Fi for the real network name.

If you must use public Wi-Fi:

  • Do not use it for banking or other sensitive information, or to make a purchase.
  • Turn Wi-Fi off when you do not need it.
  • Prefer websites that show a padlock in the address area (often a sign of a more secure HTTPS connection).
  • Watch for people reading your screen over your shoulder.

Get Cyber Safe also says that if you use public Wi-Fi often, a VPN (virtual private network) can be a safer option because it encrypts your data. Ask a tutor before you buy or install one. This course does not recommend a brand.

lessons.title: Simple habits that keep devices safer
lessons.html:
You do not need to become a security expert. A few regular habits help a lot.

1. Update your software. Get Cyber Safe says updates often add security protections, not only new features. Skipping updates can leave a device more open to malware and hacking. Turn on automatic updates when you can, for the operating system, apps, browsers, and security software. On a phone, update when the device asks, or turn on automatic updates.

2. Use strong, unique sign-ins. Get Cyber Safe recommends a passphrase of four or more random words and at least 15 characters when you can. If you use a shorter password style, use at least twelve characters with a mix of letter cases, a number, and a symbol. Use a different password for each important account. Never share a password. Do not send a password by email or text.

3. Download with care. On a computer, scan downloads with security software and delete anything it flags. On a phone, Get Cyber Safe says to install apps from trusted stores such as the App Store or Google Play, and to read the permissions an app asks for.

4. Think before you tap. Unexpected links and attachments can be risky. If a message feels wrong, do not click. Use a website you type yourself. The Range Path course Email & Online Safety Basics in Canada goes deeper on scams.

Keep a note of your device’s make and model in a safe place. If a phone is lost, Get Cyber Safe says to contact your service provider and report it to police — do not try to recover stolen property yourself.
